results.Notes: FAIL on two of ten criteria: authentic_distractors and wording_not_guessable. Both findings were formed and recorded in my Phase-1 blind lock, before any canonical content was unsealed, and are unchanged by the reveal. The item is legally correct and correctly keyed (see the companion legal record, which returns KEEP with Existing_Answer_Correct YES); the failure is one of measurement, not of law. WORDING_NOT_GUESSABLE - FALSE. The item can be answered without any legal analysis by two independent routes. (i) Answer-polarity asymmetry: the call is whether the protocol is acceptable, and exactly one option of five (C) says it is not, while A, B, D and E all validate the arrangement or excuse the pharmacist. In a single-best-answer set built around "is this permissible?", a lone negative among four permissive options is a strong structural cue and a test-wise candidate will select it on that basis alone. (ii) A conclusion-laden stem: "assigns the patient no preparation, storage, or handling role, sets no interval between the handover and the return, and runs the same way for every patient" is not a set of neutral operational facts but three consecutive assertions that the handover is a pretence. A candidate who reads that clause has been handed the answer and needs only to match it to the option containing "circumvents." A third, lesser cue compounds these: choice C's operative words "indirectly circumvents" track 247 CMR 9.01(2)'s "directly or indirectly, to circumvent" closely enough that recall of the regulation's wording substitutes for analysis. Surface cues that are sometimes responsible for guessability are absent here and were checked: option lengths are tightly matched (108, 109, 114, 122 and 124 characters, with the key at 122 and not the longest), register is uniform across the five options, and no option hedges. The guessability is structural, not cosmetic, which is why it cannot be fixed by wording tweaks alone. Compounding all of this, the stem stipulates the Massachusetts-specific legal premise - "a medication that Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer" - instead of naming a medication and making the candidate test it against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c), 105 CMR 700.003(6) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5). What remains to be tested is a single general inference about sham sequencing that a candidate with no Massachusetts knowledge can make. AUTHENTIC_DISTRACTORS - FALSE. Choice B ("The patient's possession of the syringe makes the patient rather than the pharmacist the administering party") is refuted by an express fact in the stem, which states that the protocol "has the pharmacist give the injection." A candidate can eliminate B on reading alone, with no law and no misconception to overcome, so it is a near-dead option and the item functions effectively as a four-option question. The judgement is on B alone; the other three distractors are genuine. A is the strongest and is a real formalist argument a corporate protocol author would advance, and a candidate who does not know 247 CMR 9.01(2) has no ready answer to it. D rests on a real and common misconception - conflating prescriptive and dispensing authority with administration authority - and maps onto the profile's "wrong professional scope" archetype. E rests on a belief genuinely held by staff pharmacists, that responsibility follows whoever wrote the protocol. CRITERIA ASSESSED TRUE, with reservations recorded rather than suppressed. jurisprudence_reasoning: the item requires applying a manner-based standard to an arrangement as a whole rather than to its labelled steps, which is legal reasoning; the reservation is that one of the two legal steps is stipulated away, which is scored under wording_not_guessable rather than double-counted here. practice_plausibility: the underlying situation is realistic and genuinely pharmacist-facing - service protocols are designed centrally, they are sometimes structured around a scope-of-practice limit, and a staff pharmacist asking whether the arrangement is permissible before the first clinic day is exactly the decision an MPJE candidate should be able to make; dispense-to-patient-then-administer is also a real documentary structure in practice. The reservation is that the specific choreography, with the patient carrying the syringe to the consultation room and handing it back unopened, is stylised, and no operator would commit that step to writing in the form described; that is item stylisation rather than implausibility, so it does not defeat the criterion. reasoning_not_trivia: the item turns on an inference about the function of a step, not on a recalled number, date or list. natural_rule_combination: MA-CONDUCT-ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION and MA-ADMINISTER-STATUTORY-ROUTES interlock genuinely, because an anti-circumvention analysis needs an underlying restriction to circumvent and the administration-routes rule supplies it; the reservation is that the second rule is invoked as stipulated background rather than actually exercised. appropriate_drug_context: drug_ids is empty and no medication is named, which is coherent for a professional-conduct item and introduces no clinically or legally wrong drug pairing, so nothing here is inappropriate. Two points are recorded so the finding is not read as unqualified approval: the style profile declares drug_name_usage and brand_generic_usage as characteristics of the target style, and the absence of a named medication is precisely what allows the stem to stipulate away its Massachusetts-specific step; the defect is scored where it belongs, under wording_not_guessable. not_schedule_flashcard: the item is not a controlled-substance schedule recall item; the only scheduling fact in play, that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(6) sweeps prescription drugs into Schedule VI, is background the item does not even surface. public_style_without_copying: the prose is original, the decision structure is scenario-based and consistent with the profile's familiarity_goal, and nothing is copied or lightly paraphrased from protected, recalled or commercial question wording; the item's four reasoning_steps meet the profile's difficulty-5 depth target of three. DISTINCT_FROM_BANK - TRUE, assessed against all 439 canonical records in data/questions, by family, by shared rule dependency, and by whole-bank lexical overlap over stems and options rather than by sample. Closest comparators, in order. MA-Q-0295 is the nearest: it is the only other member of family ANTI_CIRCUMVENTION_STANDARD, it is the only other item carrying MA-CONDUCT-ANTI-CIRCUMVENTION, it is likewise SBA, and it tests the same central proposition, that a sequence whose steps are each independently compliant can still violate the standard because the manner was designed to circumvent. Its key, "A violation arises, because the manner was designed to circumvent the law," is the abstract form of MA-Q-0426's key, and its distractor A ("each step in the sequence independently complies") is the abstract form of MA-Q-0426's distractor A. I nonetheless assess them as distinct rather than duplicative: MA-Q-0295 is an abstract transfer-sequence item at difficulty 4 with no administration overlay and no responsibility distractor, while MA-Q-0426 is a concrete administration scenario at difficulty 5 that adds the functionless-step analysis and the individual-versus-designer question, and pairs a second rule. Paired family members are a deliberate structure in this bank - 48 families have exactly two members and none has more - so the pairing is by design. The reservation that must be recorded is that the separation between the two items narrows considerably because MA-Q-0426 stipulates away the administration step that distinguishes it; once that premise is granted, the remaining task is the one MA-Q-0295 already sets. Any repair should therefore preserve and exercise the administration-authority reasoning, not just the circumvention reasoning. MA-Q-0359 is the only other item carrying MA-ADMINISTER-STATUTORY-ROUTES, but it is a SATA item on the differing statutory gates of the three clause (c) routes and shares no scenario or inference with MA-Q-0426. MA-Q-0422 is the nearest topical neighbour outside those rules - a pharmacist asked to administer a product outside the recognized Massachusetts administration pathways - but it turns on individual competence versus legal scope and the Department's eligible-medication list, not on circumvention by sequencing. The highest whole-bank lexical overlap was low and non-substantive: MA-Q-0173 (0.137), MA-Q-0329 (0.135), MA-Q-0111 (0.129), MA-Q-0422 and MA-Q-0114 (0.121), MA-Q-0146 (0.120); each shares only vocabulary such as administer, injection, syringe or pharmacist, and none tests this item's proposition. WHAT A REPAIR WOULD HAVE TO ACHIEVE, recorded for the controller and not performed here: replace distractor B; convert at least one further option into a wrong-reason "impermissible" option so that negative polarity no longer identifies the key; and rewrite the stem's conclusory clause into operational facts from which the absence of any independent function must be inferred. Because that touches the decisive stem clause and two of five options, the verdict is MAJOR_REWRITE rather than MINOR_EDIT. Severity is Medium, not High: nothing in the item is legally wrong or misleading, and a candidate is not taught anything false - the item simply fails to discriminate between candidates who know Massachusetts law and candidates who are test-wise. Naming the medication and requiring it to be tested against M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c), 105 CMR 700.003(6) and M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(c)(5) would repair the guessability, the stipulated-premise weakness and the narrowness of the separation from MA-Q-0295 in a single move.
